items.questionAndWhy: Can personalized risk communication based on a machine-learning risk score move an actual health behavior, and does telling people that an algorithm generated the risk assessment help or hurt?
items.whatTheyDid: Rosenbaum and colleagues ran three preregistered randomized field trials with more than 90,000 unique U.S. healthcare-system patients identified by a previously validated machine-learning model as being at high risk for influenza and related complications. Patients received no message, a simple vaccine reminder, or messages emphasizing their high-risk status; some versions disclosed algorithm involvement or gave personalized reasons for the risk prediction.
items.whatTheyFound: High-risk messages increased vaccination by 1.1–1.4 percentage points relative to a simple reminder and by 1.7–3.5 points relative to no message. Vaccination rates were similar whether messages disclosed algorithm involvement or provided personalized explanations of why the patient was considered high risk. These are randomized field effects on vaccination behavior, but only among patients already selected as high risk by the model.
items.whatItMeans: The useful ingredient was actionable personal risk information, not AI branding or explainability. This is strong evidence that an algorithm can add value upstream by identifying whom to target even when mentioning the algorithm downstream does not change behavior. It also cautions against assuming that explainability will automatically improve uptake.
items.streamTitle: Personalized high-risk flu messages increased vaccination, while disclosing the algorithm added no extra effect
items.streamSummary: Three preregistered field trials involving more than 90,000 high-risk U.S. patients tested flu-vaccination messages informed by a machine-learning risk model. Telling patients they were at high risk increased vaccination by 1.1–1.4 percentage points over a simple reminder and 1.7–3.5 points over no message. Disclosing that an algorithm identified the risk, or explaining the personalized reasons behind its prediction, did not materially change uptake. The result supports algorithm-assisted targeting and risk communication, but not the assumption that mentioning or explaining the AI itself improves behavior.
items.attribution: Rosenbaum et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.questionAndWhy: When public-hospital doctors are allowed to treat private patients, can contract design prevent them from crowding out public care, and how do clinicians adapt when the rules change?
items.whatTheyDid: Guo and colleagues analyzed 2.3 million Irish inpatient-discharge records from 2009–2015 around a 2014 reform that allowed private patients to be treated in public wards. They combined Little's Law with a difference-in-differences design. Consultant contracts required roughly three or four additional public patients for each private patient treated.
items.whatTheyFound: The reform did not increase the share of private patients. Instead, the authors found that consultants treated more public patients while shortening lengths of stay for both public and private patients. The paper concludes that the contractual ratio appears to have redirected the incentive, while also warning that the efficiency gains may have come at the expense of care quality for public patients.
items.whatItMeans: Rules shape adaptation, not just compliance. When a system constrains one profitable behavior, actors may meet the constraint by changing throughput, timing, or another margin. For policy and organizational design, intended quantity effects should therefore be evaluated alongside quality, burden, and substitution effects.
items.streamTitle: Hospital contract rules redirected incentives toward more public patients, with a possible quality tradeoff
items.streamSummary: Using 2.3 million Irish inpatient records, researchers examined a 2014 reform that let public hospitals place private patients in public wards while consultant contracts required three or four additional public patients for each private patient. The private-patient share did not increase. Instead, consultants treated more public patients and shortened stays for both groups. The authors interpret the contract ratio as an important constraint on behavior, while warning that faster throughput may have reduced care quality for public patients. The study shows why incentive evaluation must track adaptation across several outcomes, not just the behavior directly regulated.
items.attribution: Guo et al. — Nature Human Behaviour

items.questionAndWhy: Does being full reliably reduce automatic attention to high-calorie food, and does that effect differ by body-mass index or whether the food was just eaten?
items.whatTheyDid: Ballestero-Arnau and colleagues ran two emotional-attentional-blink experiments. Experiment 1 included 183 participants randomly assigned to tasting, satiation, or non-eating conditions. Experiment 2 included 61 participants in normal-weight and overweight/obesity groups and independently manipulated hunger or satiety and whether the food cue was recently consumed or novel.
items.whatTheyFound: Food distractors impaired target detection when presented close in time to the target. In Experiment 1, higher BMI predicted greater attentional bias when hungry but a smaller bias when satiated. In Experiment 2, however, participants with overweight/obesity retained strong attentional bias to novel high-calorie foods after satiation, while the bias declined in normal-weight participants. For foods that had just been eaten, attentional bias remained significant in both groups.
items.whatItMeans: Internal state does not simply switch cue-driven attention on or off. Satiety, BMI, novelty, and recent consumption interacted, and even a recently eaten food could still capture attention. That makes attentional bias a context-dependent process rather than a stable trait or straightforward proxy for hunger.
items.streamTitle: Satiety did not reliably silence attention to high-calorie foods, and BMI changed the pattern
items.streamSummary: Two attentional-blink experiments tested whether hunger, satiety, BMI, and recent food consumption change automatic capture by high-calorie food cues. Food distractors reliably disrupted target detection. After satiation, attention to novel foods declined in normal-weight participants but remained robust among participants with overweight or obesity; cues for foods that had just been eaten continued to capture attention in both groups. The findings do not show that attention causes overeating, but they demonstrate that satiety alone is not a simple off-switch for food-cue salience and that context changes the observed bias.
items.attribution: Ballestero-Arnau, Rodríguez-Herreros & Cunillera — International Journal of Obesity

items.questionAndWhy: Long-horizon agents can recover from mistakes by searching backward through earlier decisions, but when is that extra search worth its cost, and how can the policy adapt as new execution evidence arrives?
items.whatTheyDid: Zeng and colleagues introduced ForkPilot, a two-stage policy for retrospective search. It first learns the value of backtracking from completed trajectories, then updates that policy online as new trajectories accumulate. The authors evaluated it across six benchmarks, seven LLM backbone families, and nine baselines, including a production agent harness used by a large paid-user population.
items.whatTheyFound: ForkPilot achieved performance comparable to the strongest baselines while reducing token use by as much as 59.2% in the reported evaluations. The key mechanism is treating search value as dynamic: a branch that was worth revisiting earlier may become less useful as evidence accumulates. Results are benchmark and system evaluations from a preprint, not proof that the same savings will hold across all long-running agent workflows.
items.whatItMeans: More reasoning is not always better. Persistent agents need a policy for when to reconsider earlier work, when to continue forward, and when prior search estimates have become stale. That turns retrospective search into a resource-allocation problem rather than a fixed 'think harder' setting.
items.streamTitle: ForkPilot learned when agents should backtrack and cut token use by as much as 59%
items.streamSummary: ForkPilot treats retrospective search in long-horizon agents as a changing cost–benefit decision rather than a fixed behavior. It learns from completed trajectories which earlier branches were worth revisiting, then updates that policy as new executions accumulate. Across six benchmarks, seven model families, and nine baselines, the authors report state-of-the-art-comparable performance with token reductions of up to 59.2%. The work is preprint-stage and benchmark-dependent, but it highlights a practical agent-design principle: recovery, re-search, and self-correction should be allocated selectively rather than invoked uniformly.

items.questionAndWhy: How can a long-horizon agent be stopped when malicious instructions enter early, propagate through several steps, and only become dangerous when a later tool call or message is about to execute?
items.whatTheyDid: Liu and colleagues built staged prompt-injection attacks against Claude Code and Codex across eight workflow scenarios, seven attack goals, and six injection surfaces. They then formulated boundary action auditing: inspect each fully specified consequential action immediately before it executes. Their benchmark paired 479 attacked and benign executions, yielding 3,112 decision units.
items.whatTheyFound: Using Claude Sonnet 5 as the audit backend, their Path-Aligned Attribution method reached 86% block recall at a 6–8% false-block rate. The ARGUS comparison reached 44–47% recall at 16–33% false-block rates; on tool calls jointly supported by other auditors, the proposed method also outperformed the comparisons. These are controlled preprint results and depend on the tested workflows, attack generator, and audit backend.
items.whatItMeans: For tool-using agents, the last safe decision point may be the boundary just before an external effect occurs. Security controls that only scan initial inputs or review a completed run can miss attacks whose meaning emerges across the trajectory. Consequential actions should therefore carry provenance and be independently checked before execution.
items.streamTitle: Pre-action boundary auditing blocked substantially more staged prompt injections in long-horizon agents
items.streamSummary: Researchers generated staged prompt-injection attacks that propagate through multi-step Claude Code and Codex workflows and only become harmful at a later consequential action. They then audited the pending message or tool call immediately before execution. On a 479-pair benchmark, Path-Aligned Attribution reached 86% block recall at a 6–8% false-block rate, compared with 44–47% recall and 16–33% false-block rates for ARGUS under the same backend. The work is preprint-stage, but it supports a clear security pattern: trace where action parameters came from and gate external effects at the execution boundary.

items.questionAndWhy: Can a robot trained on familiar dual-arm skills recombine them in new orders and synchronized patterns, rather than memorizing fixed two-arm routines?
items.whatTheyDid: Zhang and colleagues introduced ACG-Bench with 23 task-condition pairs across eight task families: six in-domain conditions and 17 unseen skill compositions. Using the same vision-language-action backbone and source data, they compared data and architecture strategies including arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters, and arm-wise attention, then combined them in AE-VLA.
items.whatTheyFound: AE-VLA reached 21.53% generalization success in simulation versus 5.53% for the strongest reported baseline. On physical SO101 robots, it averaged 39% success across five unseen conditions versus 10% for the strongest baseline. The relative improvement is large, but the absolute success rates remain low enough that the system is not robust for unsupervised real-world deployment.
items.whatItMeans: Compositional generalization can improve when model structure mirrors the problem structure—in this case, separating per-arm skills while coordinating their interaction. The remaining failure rate is just as important as the relative gain and should remain visible when interpreting robotics benchmarks.
items.streamTitle: Arm-structured policies improved dual-arm robot generalization, while absolute success remained limited
items.streamSummary: ACG-Bench tests whether dual-arm robots can recombine familiar per-arm skills in unseen orders and timing relationships. An architecture combining skill-specific adapters and arm-wise attention reached 21.53% success on unseen simulated compositions versus 5.53% for the strongest baseline, and 39% on five physical-robot conditions versus 10% for the strongest baseline. The relative improvement is substantial, but most unseen physical trials still failed. The study therefore supports arm-aware architectural structure as a promising generalization strategy without implying that dual-arm compositional autonomy is solved.

items.questionAndWhy: How is NATO testing whether its command structure can execute regional collective-defense plans across multiple domains while experimenting with newer concepts and AI-enabled exercise tools?
items.whatTheyDid: NATO began STEADFAST DUEL 2026, its largest annual computer-assisted command-post exercise, involving about 8,000 military and civilian personnel, all 32 Allies, NATO headquarters, U.S. European Command, and multiple command elements. The simulated Article 5 environment covers land, air, maritime, space, cyber, electronic warfare, CBRN defense, logistics, and civil-military coordination.
items.whatTheyFound: The exercise is also being used for experimentation on multi-domain operations implementation, cognitive warfare, escalation dynamics, and NATO Maven Smart System capabilities under the AI in Audacious Training initiative. The meaningful fact today is the breadth of what NATO is testing; the exercise has not yet produced public evidence that these experiments improve readiness, decision quality, interoperability, or operational outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: Training events are becoming testbeds for doctrine, organization, AI, and command-and-control design at the same time. The follow-on evidence should distinguish successful exercise execution from demonstrated improvement by measuring decision speed, coordination quality, error rates, interoperability, and what changed because of the experimental capability.
items.streamTitle: NATO is using STEADFAST DUEL 2026 to test Article 5 command structures, cognitive warfare, and AI-enabled training
items.streamSummary: STEADFAST DUEL 2026 brings about 8,000 personnel and all 32 NATO Allies into the Alliance's largest annual computer-assisted command-post exercise. The Article 5 scenario tests multi-domain command and control across land, air, maritime, space, cyber, electronic warfare, logistics, CBRN defense, and civil-military coordination. NATO is also using the event to experiment with cognitive warfare, escalation dynamics, and its Maven Smart System. The exercise demonstrates an integrated testing environment, not yet improved readiness: public results on decision quality, interoperability, or operational effect have not been reported.

items.questionAndWhy: How do U.S. voters currently perceive AI risks and government oversight, and are those concerns confined to one political party or spread across the electorate?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters/Ipsos conducted a six-day nationwide online survey ending October 5 with 4,506 U.S. adults, including 3,526 registered voters. The reported margin of error for the voter findings was about two percentage points. Questions covered government handling of AI, employment, regulation, data centers, catastrophic risk, and military targeting.
items.whatTheyFound: Among registered voters, 57% said the Trump administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough or at all, and 54% said the same of Congress. Eighty-four percent saw AI as a threat to American workers; 80% of Democrats and 61% of Republicans supported stricter AI regulation. Fifty-six percent supported limits on data-center construction, and 57% opposed using AI to determine the target of a military strike, up from 49% in an August 2025 Reuters/Ipsos poll.
items.whatItMeans: AI governance has a broad public-opinion component that cuts across several issue areas rather than one generic attitude toward technology. For strategy and communication, employment, infrastructure, safety, and military use should be treated as distinct concerns. This survey measures expressed attitudes at one point in time, not actual policy preferences under specific tradeoffs or future voting behavior.
items.streamTitle: U.S. voters showed broad concern about AI jobs, regulation, data centers, and military targeting
items.streamSummary: A nationwide Reuters/Ipsos survey of 4,506 adults found broad concern about AI across party lines. Among registered voters, 57% said the administration was not taking AI risks seriously enough, 84% saw AI as a threat to American workers, and majorities of Democrats and Republicans supported stricter regulation. Fifty-six percent backed limits on data-center construction, while 57% opposed using AI to determine military-strike targets, up from 49% in an August 2025 poll. The survey captures current attitudes, not how voters would respond to detailed policy tradeoffs or how concerns translate into behavior.

items.questionAndWhy: If an LLM is asked to stand in for a particular survey respondent, what information actually helps it reproduce that person's later choices rather than merely matching population averages?
items.whatTheyDid: Pourtaheri and Zareei used a two-wave panel of 845 U.S. adults who completed measures of 14 behavioral biases spanning risk, time preference, overconfidence, and reasoning. Synthetic personas received progressively richer information: none, demographics, personality, cognitive scores, or the respondent's earlier survey choices, while items directly scoring the target bias were withheld.
items.whatTheyFound: All persona conditions reproduced the population-average number of biases fairly well, but description-based personas recovered only 53–67% of human between-person variation. Adding behavioral history restored aggregate variance to roughly the human level. At the individual level, demographics/personality/cognitive descriptions achieved only 7–12% of human test–retest informedness, while behavioral history reached up to 28%. Synthetic responses also exaggerated education- and income-related differences relative to humans.
items.whatItMeans: Population-level similarity can hide poor person-level fidelity. For synthetic-persona research, observed behavioral history is much more informative than descriptive attributes, but even the best condition remained far below human self-consistency at the individual level. Synthetic respondents should therefore be validated against the level of inference they are meant to support.
items.streamTitle: Behavioral history beat demographics and personality for predicting individual synthetic-persona choices
items.streamSummary: A two-wave study of 845 U.S. adults tested what information helps LLM synthetic personas reproduce a particular person's later decisions across 14 behavioral biases. Demographics, personality, and cognitive descriptions produced population averages that looked human-like but captured only 7–12% of human test–retest informedness at the individual level. Supplying earlier behavioral choices raised that figure to as much as 28% and restored between-person variance much more effectively. The result supports behavioral history as a stronger persona scaffold, while also showing that even richer synthetic personas remain weak substitutes for specific individuals.

items.questionAndWhy: What evidence is being used to support European approval of Tesla's Full Self-Driving (Supervised), and does that evidence justify public claims that the system prevents deaths?
items.whatTheyDid: Reuters reviewed hundreds of pages of correspondence between Tesla and European regulators, examined Tesla safety studies circulated to regulators, and asked seven traffic-safety researchers to assess the methodology. The European study compared FSD vehicles driven by professional engineering drivers with ordinary owner-driven Teslas, but had too few FSD miles for a meaningful crash-rate comparison, so it used surrogate behaviors such as hard braking, emergency braking, horn use, turn-signal use, acceleration, and cornering.
items.whatTheyFound: The interviewed researchers said several surrogate measures were weak indicators of crash risk and that the study did not provide evidence that FSD prevents fatal crashes. Tesla's own fine print said the comparisons should not be interpreted as causal estimates. Reuters also found that Tesla pressed Dutch regulators to reduce parts of the review burden and that the regulator accommodated some requests; the Dutch regulator said its evaluation remained objective and independent.
items.whatItMeans: A safety case can fail at the link between proxy and outcome even when the proxy is measured precisely. This is a useful governance example of why surrogate validity, comparison-group selection, exposure denominators, causal wording, independent review, and regulator independence all need to be visible before a technical performance claim becomes a public safety claim.
items.streamTitle: Tesla's European FSD safety evidence did not support its strongest life-saving claims, outside researchers told Reuters
items.streamSummary: A Reuters investigation reviewed Tesla's European FSD safety studies, regulatory correspondence, and assessments from seven traffic-safety researchers. Because the company had too few European FSD miles for a meaningful crash-rate comparison, it relied on surrogate behaviors such as hard braking, horn use, turn signals, acceleration, and cornering. Researchers said several proxies were weak and the evidence did not show that FSD prevents fatal crashes; Tesla's own study cautioned that the comparisons were not causal estimates. Reuters also documented pressure on Dutch regulators, who said their review remained independent. The case highlights the difference between measured proxies and validated safety outcomes.
